bib.title: Agyn: A Multi-Agent System for Team-Based Autonomous Software Engineering

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Agyn: A Multi-Agent System for Team-Based Autonomous Software Engineering", Nikita Benkovich and Vitalii Valkov (Agyn; Mila e-Lab, Tel-Aviv). Preprint, "Under review", arXiv:2602.01465v2, 7 Feb 2026.
COVERAGE: all 10 of 10 pages, 41,713 chars; the text I read ran through the Section 5 limits and the start of the references. I did not read the rest of the reference list. There are no appendices. No figures were extracted.

CORE CLAIM: Modelling issue resolution as an engineering team gives a competitive SWE-bench result. The team is a manager, researcher, engineer and reviewer, each in its own sandbox, with a methodology and an approve-PR gate. The authors say organisational design may matter as much as model gains. This is a hypothesis, not something the paper tests.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
- 72.2% resolved on SWE-bench 500 (text-only). Setup: manager and researcher on GPT-5 (medium reasoning); engineer and reviewer on GPT-5-Codex (medium). Fixed config, no benchmark tuning, no human intervention. A task counts only if the reviewer agent approves the PR. The paper does not state the number of runs (it looks like one), and it reports no cost or token figures.
- Table 1 (p8), GPT-5-family systems: agyn 72.2; OpenHands + GPT-5 71.8; mini-SWE-agent + GPT-5.2 (high) 71.8; mini-SWE-agent + GPT-5 (medium) 65.0.
- The headline "7.4% higher than mini-SWE-agent" (p3) is 72.2 vs 65.0, in absolute points, against the GPT-5 medium baseline only. The gap to OpenHands is 0.4 points and to mini-SWE-agent + GPT-5.2 (high) it is 0.4. mini-SWE-agent + Gemini 3 Pro Preview scores 74.2, which beats Agyn.

ABLATION: None. There is no single-agent vs multi-agent comparison on the same models and no per-role ablation. Role, sandbox and model allocation are never isolated. The comparison is against other published systems with different scaffolds.

DESIGN FACTS USEFUL FOR NOTE 07
- Hub-and-spoke topology: "Agents ... do not communicate directly with each other." All traffic goes through the manager's `manage` tool, chosen for simpler control flow and traceability (p5-6).
- Role-based model allocation: large models for research and management, smaller code models for implementation (p2, p5).
- Per-agent isolated sandboxes, so failed attempts are discarded without side effects (p5).
- Objective acceptance gate: done only when the reviewer approves the PR. The manager must call a `finish` tool, and a separate `send_message` tool keeps chat out of control flow (p6-7).
- Context controls: shell output over 50,000 tokens goes to a file and the agent gets a reference. The history is auto-summarised at a threshold.
- The GitHub MCP integration bloated context with metadata and hurt performance, so they moved to the `gh` CLI plus a custom `gh-pr-review` extension (p6).

QUOTES
- "Agents in our system do not communicate directly with each other. Instead, coordination is explicitly mediated by the manager agent through a dedicated manage tool." (p5)
- "a task is considered complete only when a pull request has been approved by the reviewer agent, rather than when an agent produces a natural language completion message." (p6)
- "At times, the manager agent waited for actions from other agents that had already completed their work, leading to stalled execution." (p10)
- "clear communication contracts are essential for stable multi-agent collaboration." (p10)

LIMITS
- No ablation, so the claim that team structure causes the gain is untested. Model differences (GPT-5-Codex for two roles) and the extra reviewer loop are confounded with structure.
- The paper reports no cost, latency or token comparison, even though it frames cost efficiency as a goal. It gives no number of runs or variance.
- The authors say small leaderboard gaps "should therefore be interpreted with caution", and that scores cluster at 70-75%.
- Interrupted runs were resumed from persisted GitHub state (p8). Agents were told to deprioritise unrelated CI failures, which departs from normal practice (p9). The paper does not say how many tasks were resumed.
- They ran on a single MacBook Pro and hit OOM failures at high parallelism (p9).
- Failure modes reported: trajectory dependence on early environment errors, over-engineering beyond the gold patch, test timeouts, and manager stalls.
- It never discusses when not to go multi-agent. It is a single-vendor paper from the platform's authors, not peer reviewed.

BUILDS ON (as printed): SWE-bench, Jimenez et al., 2024. SWE-agent, Yang et al., 2024. mini-SWE-agent, SWE-agent Team, 2024. OpenHands, Wang et al., 2024. Self-evolving agents, Xia et al., 2025. TRAE, Gao et al., 2025 (pipeline). Prometheus, Chen et al., 2025 (pipeline, arXiv:2507.19942).

FIGURES: None extracted (Table 1 on p8 is the only exhibit). No figure candidate. I did not run the captions script.

FIT: Weak to moderate for 07-orchestration. It is an industry case study, so cite it as one example, not as evidence. Fit by topic:
- Role separation and manager-centric topology: yes. It is a clean production example of hub-and-spoke with separate model tiers.
- Handoff and communication contracts, plus the stalled-manager failure: a modest data point.
- Context firewall: only partly. Sandboxes and output-to-file are shown, but without measurement.
- Not a basis for "multi-agent beats single-agent": the paper has no controlled comparison.
- The 50k-token output-to-file rule and the MCP-vs-CLI context-bloat finding fit 02-context-engineering or 03-tool-design better.

PROBLEMS: None. The extraction was clean and there were no embedded instructions.
